title: the breath again — every claim checked
hook: the senses quarrel over who holds the body up, and breath settles it by getting up to leave
carry: the breath again — every claim checked
tomorrow: the breath again — every claim checked

segments.voice: Last time, the breath again, with a promise attached: every claim checked. Did you catch yourself breathing at some point since, without trying to change it? Day one thousand three hundred twenty-two.

An argument breaks out inside a body. Speech says it holds the body up. So does the mind. So do the eye and the ear. Each one is sure it's the pillar. Then breath, the quiet one, says nothing much. It just starts to leave. And the moment it lifts, every other power is dragged up with it, whether it likes it or not. This story sits in the second question of the Prashna Upanishad, a text built as six students asking a teacher six questions. Today: what the old texts mean by breath, and one popular claim about it, checked against the page.
screen: `AN ARGUMENT INSIDE A BODY.` → `BREATH STARTS TO LEAVE.` → `ONE CLAIM, CHECKED AGAINST THE PAGE.`

segments.voice: Here is the scene, in paraphrase. A student asks the teacher Pippalada which powers hold a being together, and which of them is greatest. The teacher tells the quarrel. The elements and the senses each claim the body. Breath warns them not to be fooled: it alone, dividing itself, keeps the body standing. They don't believe it. So breath rises to go, and they all rise with it. It settles, and they all settle. The text gives the picture: bees following their king bee out of the hive, and back when he comes back. After that, the senses sing to breath, and the hymn makes it very large. Breath burns as fire, shines as the sun, falls as rain. Breath is in everything. Now the claim. One line you'll hear in wellness writing says prana is basically oxygen. Another says it's a hidden energy that a machine can read. Check both against this chapter. The first is too small. The Prashna's breath is fire and rain and the life of creatures, not one gas in the lungs. The second is a different kind of claim altogether. The Upanishad never offers prana as something to measure. It offers a way of seeing a living thing as held together by something it doesn't control. That's the line these days hold to, and the chapter bears it out: read prana as a teaching about life, and don't sell it as a reading on a dial. What a person can actually watch is the breath itself, going out and coming back. The Prashna asks for nothing more than that.
screen: `THE SENSES EACH CLAIM THE BODY` · `BEES FOLLOWING THEIR KING BEE` · `BREATH AS FIRE, SUN AND RAIN` · `A TEACHING, NOT A READING ON A DIAL`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: let breath be the one that holds you up. Sit comfortably. Don't steer the breath; just notice it rising and settling. As it rises, notice what rises with it: the chest, the shoulders, maybe a thought. As it settles, notice what settles. Speech is quiet. The eyes can rest. Let the breath be the king bee, and everything else the swarm that follows. If you pray, you can offer one breath back with thanks. The bell holds the time.
The breath again. In the Prashna, breath gets up to leave and every other power rises with it, like bees with their king. Today's word.
Your line: the breath again — every claim checked. Today, when someone tells you what prana is, ask which text says so. Day one thousand three hundred twenty-two.

howItsDone: Hindu teachers read the Prashna Upanishad's quarrel of the senses as a teaching about what keeps a being alive, and some Hindus sit with the breath as a daily practice of attention.

fork.setup: you're breath. speech, mind, eye and ear all insist they hold the body up, and they won't listen. what do you do?
options: argue louder than all of them.
start to leave, and let them feel it.
agree with them to keep the peace.
fork.reveal: breath rises to go, and every other power is pulled up with it. they believe it then, and sing to breath.

original.note: Sanskrit: breath, life. in the Prashna Upanishad's second question, the power the senses finally praise.

trapdoor: what you thought: prana is a fancy word for oxygen.
what it means: in the Prashna, breath holds the body together, and the senses rise and fall with it.
what a scholar hears: the same hymn makes breath fire, sun and rain, so prana names life itself, not one gas.

notes: Day 1321 was not on disk when this was written; the review is kept general. Check that day 1321 did not already use the Prashna's quarrel of the senses (the Chandogya 5.1 and Brihadaranyaka 6.1 versions of the contest were deliberately avoided here, but check overlap).
Prashna 2.1: the student asking is Bhargava Vaidarbhi; confirm the question as paraphrased ('which powers hold a being together, and which is greatest').
Prashna 2.3–4: confirm the paraphrase that breath says it divides itself to support the body, and the image of bees following the king bee (madhukara-raja).
Prashna 2.5–13: confirm 'fire, sun, rain' as examples from the hymn to prana.
Science-seat line: the lesson treats the 'prana is oxygen' and 'prana is measurable energy' claims as not supported by the text; it does not make any scientific claim of its own. Check wording.
'Six students, six questions' is the frame of the Prashna (1.1); confirm.
